stimulus.title: Nitrate and dawn dissolved oxygen at five stream sites
stimulus.text: A stream flows through a forest (site A), then past fertilized cornfields (site B), and on through more forest (sites C to E). Students measured nitrate and dissolved oxygen (DO) at dawn at each site on five mornings in a dry week of July, and again on five mornings in July two weeks after a week of heavy rain. Water temperature was 18-19 °C at every site on every morning. Values are means ± 2 SE (n = 5 mornings).

table.caption: Nitrate (mg/L) and dissolved oxygen at dawn (mg/L, mean ± 2 SE)

checks: bar graph with site on the x-axis
y-axis labeled dissolved oxygen with units (mg/L)
linear scale from 0 that uses most of the grid
both sampling periods plotted with a key
error bars of ±2 SE on every bar

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how nitrate washed from the cornfields can increase the growth of algae in the stream.

rubric.point: Describes that nitrogen is a limiting nutrient for algae; algae use nitrate to make amino acids/proteins and nucleic acids, so more nitrate lets them grow and divide faster (an algal bloom).
accept: nitrogen limits algal growth, so adding nitrate lets algae multiply
algae take up nitrate to build proteins and DNA, so they grow faster
extra nitrate removes a limiting factor, causing an algal bloom

parts.sample: Algae need nitrogen to build amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids, and in this stream nitrogen limits their growth. Nitrate from the fields removes that limit, so the algae grow and divide faster and can form a bloom.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Construct an appropriately labeled graph that shows the mean dissolved oxygen at dawn at each site for both sampling periods, including error bars.

rubric.point: Bar graph (or points) with site on the x-axis and dissolved oxygen on the y-axis.
accept: sites A-E on the x-axis, DO on the y-axis
bars for each site
correct graph type with correct axes

rubric.point: Axes labeled, with units on the DO axis (mg/L), and a linear scale starting at 0.
accept: y-axis: dissolved oxygen at dawn (mg/L)
labels on both axes and units
evenly spaced scale from 0

rubric.point: All ten means plotted correctly, with a key that distinguishes the dry week from after rain.
accept: two bars per site, shaded differently, with a legend
both data sets plotted accurately
key identifies the two sampling periods

rubric.point: Error bars of ±2 SE drawn on every mean.
accept: error bars from mean − 2 SE to mean + 2 SE
for example 3.2 ± 0.6 drawn from 2.6 to 3.8
all ten error bars correct

parts.sample: A bar graph with sites A-E on the x-axis and "Dissolved oxygen at dawn (mg/L)" on the y-axis, scaled 0 to 10 in steps of 1. Each site has two bars, one for the dry week and one for after rain, identified in a key. Each bar has an error bar of ±2 SE, for example site D after rain from 2.6 to 3.8 mg/L.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt:
(i) Justify the students' choice of site A as part of the study.
(ii) Using the error bars, determine whether dissolved oxygen at site D differs between the dry week and after the rain, and justify your answer.

rubric.point: (i) Site A is above the farms, so it receives no runoff from them: it is a control/reference that shows the stream's DO and nitrate without farm inputs, so changes downstream can be attributed to the farms.
accept: a control site upstream of the fields
shows natural conditions in the stream for comparison
rules out that rain itself (without farm runoff) changed DO

rubric.point: (ii) Yes, they differ: 7.6 ± 0.4 (7.2-8.0) and 3.2 ± 0.6 (2.6-3.8) do not overlap.
accept: the error bars do not overlap, so the difference is significant
7.2-8.0 and 2.6-3.8 are far apart
DO after rain is clearly lower at site D

parts.sample: (i) Site A is upstream of the cornfields, so it gets no runoff from them. It is a control that shows the stream's normal nitrate and oxygen in each period; because DO there barely changed after the rain (8.6 vs 8.4), the drops downstream can be linked to the farm runoff rather than to the rain itself. (ii) They differ. In the dry week the interval is 7.2-8.0 mg/L; after rain it is 2.6-3.8 mg/L. The intervals do not overlap, so the drop is unlikely to be due to chance.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt:
(i) Nitrate after the rain was highest at site C, but dawn DO was lowest at site D. Explain why the lowest oxygen occurs farther downstream than the highest nitrate.
(ii) The farmers plant 20-meter strips of grass and trees between the fields and the stream. Predict the effect on dawn DO at site D after heavy rain, and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: (i) Explains the time lag as water flows downstream: algae need time to grow on the nitrate, then die, and decomposers then use O₂ (and algae respire at night) as they break down the algae, so the oxygen low develops downstream of the nutrient peak.
accept: it takes time for the bloom to grow, die and be decomposed, while the water keeps moving
decomposition of the algae, which uses oxygen, happens after the algae have grown, farther downstream
the water carries the algae downstream as they grow; their respiration and decay use O₂ there

rubric.point: (ii) Predicts that DO at site D will be higher (less of a drop) after rain, because the plants take up nitrate (and slow runoff) before it reaches the stream, so fewer algae grow and less O₂ is used in respiration and decomposition.
accept: higher DO, because the buffer strips absorb nitrate and less reaches the stream
less of an oxygen drop, because fewer nutrients mean a smaller algal bloom and less decay
DO will stay closer to the dry-week level because runoff is filtered by the vegetation

parts.sample: (i) The nitrate does not lower oxygen directly. Algae first take it up and multiply, which takes days, while the water keeps flowing downstream. As the bloom ages, algae respire at night and many die, and decomposers use O₂ to break them down. These oxygen-using steps happen farther along the stream, so the lowest dawn DO is at site D, after the nitrate peak at C. (ii) Dawn DO at site D will be higher after heavy rain than it was. The roots of the grass and trees take up nitrate, and the strips slow runoff, so less nitrate reaches the stream; fewer algae grow, and less oxygen is used by their respiration and decomposition.
